content: Typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever are two closely related illnesses caused by different types of bacteria. Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella Typhi, while paratyphoid fever is caused by Salmonella Paratyphi. These bacteria are transmitted from person to person, typically through the fecal-oral route. This means that an infected individual who does not wash their hands properly after using the bathroom can contaminate surfaces, food, or drinks that others may come into contact with. In areas with poor sanitation, water used for food preparation or drinking, including tap water, can also become contaminated with these bacteria. Travelers who consume contaminated food or beverages are at risk of becoming infected. The symptoms of typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever are similar. Affected individuals often experience a high fever, which can reach 103–104°F (39–40°C). Other symptoms may include weakness, abdominal pain, headache, diarrhea or constipation, cough, and loss of appetite. In some cases, a rash with flat, rose-colored spots may appear. Although rare, complications such as internal bleeding or death can occur. Typhoid and paratyphoid fever are most prevalent in regions where food and water safety is compromised, and sanitation is inadequate. These diseases are particularly common in parts of Eastern and Southern Asia, including Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh, as well as in Africa, the Caribbean, Central and South America, and the Middle East. Travelers visiting friends or relatives in these regions are at higher risk because they may stay for extended periods, consume home-prepared local foods, and may not take precautions such as vaccination before traveling. In the United States, approximately 425 cases of typhoid fever and 125 cases of paratyphoid fever are reported annually, with most cases linked to international travel. To prevent typhoid fever, travelers should consider vaccination, practice careful food and drink selection, and maintain good hand hygiene. Two types of typhoid vaccines are available in the United States: 1. Oral vaccine (pill form): This vaccine is suitable for individuals aged 6 years and older. It requires taking four pills, one every other day, and completing the course at least one week before travel. 2. Injectable vaccine (shot form): This vaccine is recommended for individuals aged 2 years and older. A single shot should be administered at least two weeks before travel. It is important to note that typhoid vaccines are only 50–80% effective, and there is no vaccine available for paratyphoid fever. Therefore, travelers must also take additional precautions to reduce their risk of infection. Food and drink precautions: Consume only foods that are thoroughly cooked and served hot. Avoid food that has been sitting out, such as on a buffet. Eat raw fruits and vegetables only if they have been washed in clean water or peeled. Drink only beverages from factory-sealed containers. Avoid ice, as it may be made from contaminated water. Consume only pasteurized milk. Hand hygiene: Wash hands frequently with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially after using the bathroom and before eating. If soap and water are unavailable, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer containing at least 60% alcohol. Avoid touching your face and mouth with unwashed hands.
